description: This topic covers the identification, nomenclature, and classification of living organisms in Biology. It is a highly crucial and fundamental section for competitive exams.

sections.title: Basic Principles of Taxonomy
sections.description: The scientific process of grouping organisms based on their similarities and differences.

key_concepts.explanation: The branch of biology that deals with the identification, nomenclature (naming), and classification of organisms.
The descending order of different levels of classification. The sequence is: Kingdom -> Phylum -> Class -> Order -> Family -> Genus -> Species.
It is the smallest and most basic unit of classification. Organisms of the same species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
A formal system of naming species of living things by giving each a name composed of two parts. The first part indicates the Genus and the second part indicates the Species (e.g., Homo sapiens).

sections.title: History of Classification Systems
sections.description: Various systems developed by scientists over time to categorize living organisms.

historical_events.significance: Aristotle was the first to classify organisms into two main groups based on the presence or absence of red blood. He is known as the 'Father of Biology' and 'Father of Zoology'.
Carl Linnaeus, in his book 'Systema Naturae', divided all living organisms into two broad kingdoms: Plantae (Plants) and Animalia (Animals).
R. H. Whittaker proposed the modern 5-kingdom classification based on cell structure, body organization, mode of nutrition, and phylogenetic relationships.

sections.title: Whittaker's Five Kingdom System
sections.description: The most widely accepted and used classification system in modern biology.

key_concepts.explanation: Includes all unicellular prokaryotic organisms that lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Examples: Bacteria, Cyanobacteria (Blue-green algae).
Includes all unicellular eukaryotic organisms. They are primarily aquatic. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena.
Multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic organisms that absorb their food. Their cell walls are made of chitin. Examples: Yeast (unicellular exception), Mushrooms, Molds.
Multicellular, eukaryotic, autotrophic organisms that perform photosynthesis. Their cell walls are made of cellulose.
Multicellular, eukaryotic, heterotrophic consumers. Their cells lack cell walls and plastids (chloroplasts).

sections.title: Exam-Oriented Important Facts
sections.description: Direct one-liner facts and superlative data points related to biological classification.

important_facts.fact: Carl Linnaeus is universally recognized as the 'Father of Taxonomy'.
Viruses do not find a place in Whittaker's Five-Kingdom system because they are considered a connecting link between living and non-living things (they are non-cellular).
Euglena is considered the connecting link between plants and animals because it behaves as an autotroph in sunlight (has chlorophyll) and a heterotroph in the dark.
The scientific study of fungi is called 'Mycology', and the study of algae is called 'Phycology'.
Lichens represent a mutualistic symbiotic relationship between algae and fungi, and they are excellent natural indicators of air pollution (especially Sulfur Dioxide - SO2).
